source.authors: Brandon A. Güell, Karen M. Warkentin
source.title: When and where to hatch? Red-eyed treefrog embryos use light cues in two contexts

method: behavioural: direction of hatching out of a tube with one end illuminated (half-dark cup), single embryos
conditions: Wild-collected egg masses (0-3 days old, Experimental Pond, Gamboa, Panama); individual 3-day-old eggs placed in a clear tube in the wall of a half-dark cup, one side lit and one dark, alternating the side of insertion (alternated, not randomised); hatching phototaxis tested at 4 days of age between 12:00 and 17:00; 92 embryos from 39 clutches tested in half-dark cups, 85 analysed (seven trials eliminated because eggs slipped out of their tubes when flooded); up to 3 siblings per clutch, 10 to 15 trials run concurrently in eight sets, 4 to 20 July 2015; overall 59 of 85 hatched toward the light (69.4%), chi-square = 12.047, df = 1, p < 0.001 (Results); no difference between the two sets of illuminated trials (higher and lower illumination, LED lights about 10 cm for trials 1-50 or 15-20 cm for trials 51-92; chi-square = 0.611, df = 1, p = 0.434); light intensity was not measured in this experiment (authors' statement); hatching induced by gently flooding the cups with hypoxic water. Side-bias control: 20 further embryos from 5 clutches tested in a dark room after 20 min dark acclimation, observed under dim red light, hatched 9 toward the open 'light' side and 11 toward the covered 'dark' side (chi-square = 0.05, df = 1, p = 0.823), so the cup structure gave no side bias without illumination. A separate timing experiment in the same paper (photoperiod, continuous light, continuous dark) is not used here.
value: most tested embryos hatched toward the light (59 of 85 in the Results; illumination not measured)
quote: Most embryos hatched toward the light, suggesting they use light as a directional cue.
note: The paper states that embryos at this stage 'have large, well developed eyes' and calls the test 'hatching phototaxis' for 'light or visual cues'; it does not identify the photoreceptors or address image perception. Filed under behaviour_vision (audit 332 ruling: main files phototaxis by eyed animals under behaviour_vision, and its animal sense_light_nonvisual rows are extraocular, pineal/parietal, brain or dermal light sensing). ASW lists the species as Agalychnis callidryas (Cope, 1862) under Phyllomedusidae. Family Phyllomedusidae follows main's Thomas et al. 2022 rows for this species (another main row says Hylidae); name Agalychnis callidryas accepted in GBIF per docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. source.authors: Cutter J. Barrus, Kaiyuan Zheng, Britney A. Bender, Charlotte A. Fraley, Bradley P. Roth, Sophia M. Glennie, Rowyn P. Birdsley, Kara G. Pratt
source.title: Individual Xenopus Tadpoles Display Distinct and Consistent Visual Preferences

method: behavioural: single tadpoles tested for 15 min in a dish with one quadrant (25%) shown a test stimulus against the other 75%, retested the next day
conditions: Laboratory-bred tadpoles from in-house matings of wild-type X. laevis; developmental stages 48-49; stimuli displayed on a back-lit monitor and defined by Lab colour values (white L = 100, dark L = 0, green L = 75, a = -75, b = 75), light intensity not reported (the authors note all stimuli include some backlight but relative brightness is preserved; page summary); tested in an unlit room on an LCD monitor, 1 min acclimation then 15 min recorded at 60 fps; tadpoles reared on 12:12 light/dark at 22 C, at least 3 clutches per test group, normally swimming stage 48 tadpoles chosen at random (page summary); each tadpole tested 15 min on one test and retested about 24 h later on the same test; light v dark n = 19, green v light n = 23 (two outliers excluded from the statistics); preference index scores ranged from 0.15 to 0.94 (light v dark) and 0.11 to 1.0 (green v light); the Results give no group-level test statistic for baseline preference (the abstract text 'most tadpoles preferred light' and 'majority preferred green over light' is not tested in the passages read); inter-clutch variability statistically nonsignificant; drug experiments (pCPA, fluoxetine) not used here; within-individual stability by intraclass correlation (two-way absolute-agreement, single measure; page summary): light v dark ICC 0.651 (95% CI 0.295 to 0.849), green v light ICC 0.717 (95% CI 0.445 to 0.869) (Figure 2 and 3 legends), i.e. moderate test-retest agreement; light v dark and green v light indices not significantly correlated (r = -0.235, p = 0.228, n = 28; page summary); the authors state the analyses were not corrected for multiple comparisons, 'which renders the results strictly exploratory'.
value: preferences varied across tadpoles and were stable within individuals over time (green v light and light v dark tests)
quote: While preferences varied across tadpoles, preferences displayed within individuals were stable over time (i.e., consistent).
note: The abstract also reports that some tadpoles strongly preferred green over light while others preferred light over green (sentence over 40 words, not quoted). Sentence returned verbatim in two abutting pieces in one response (audit 332). Lab-bred wild-type X. laevis accepted at species rank (audit 332; as desk-d221:5). Family and order from main (canon-2 rows for Xenopus laevis). Licence: page metadata CC BY 3.0; Crossref CC BY 4.0, content-version vor. Printed year 2026 (Crossref issued 2026-09-01).

source.authors: Seiya Tsujiuchi, Elena Sivan-Loukianova, Daniel F. Eberl, Yasuo Kitagawa, Tatsuhiko Kadowaki
source.title: Dynamic Range Compression in the Honey Bee Auditory System toward Waggle Dance Sounds

method: electrophysiology: JO sound-evoked potentials from the antennal nerve against flagellar tip displacement calculated from laser-vibrometer-measured vibration velocity (displacement = velocity/2πf)
conditions: Extracellular sound-evoked potentials (SEPs) recorded from the antennal nerve with the flagellar vibration velocity measured by laser Doppler vibrometer (CLV-700) and the air particle velocity by a near-field probe (Microflown); the tip and air particle displacements in the quote were calculated from these velocities (displacement = velocity/2πf). Bees: SEPs were recorded from pollen foragers of unknown age unless otherwise noted (Methods); known-age bees (newly emerged bees collected from combs isolated from a hive, marked and returned) were used for the age comparison (Fig. 8); colony, location and subspecies not stated (managed hive, accepted under audit 314). Recordings for each stimulus and age taken from at least 5 animals (Methods). Control: SEPs were no longer detectable after pedicel lesion, so they are attributable to the Johnston's organ (JO). JO responses were lower in newly eclosed (0-day) bees than in 21-day-old foragers; Fig. 6 states no age, so under the Methods default the 20 nm threshold is from pollen foragers of unknown age; N = 5 antennae per treatment (Fig. 6 legend, page summary). Responses saturate at flagellar tip displacement above 200 nm at 265 Hz (Fig. 6 legend). No temperature reported; no formal statistical test reported (error bars SE; page summary).
value: minimum JO response detected at 20 nm flagellar tip displacement (60 nm air particle displacement)
quote: The minimum response of JO neurons can be detected by 20 nm displacement of the flagellar tip (achieved by 60 nm air particle displacement, Fig. 6D).
note: Johnston's organ (antennal) detection of near-field particle displacement, not far-field pressure hearing. The abstract says the flagellum 'is a sensitive movement detector responding to 20 nm tip displacement, which is comparable to female mosquito'. Sentence returned by the page tool in two abutting pieces in one response (said in pieces). Family and order from main (Apis mellifera rows are Apidae, Hymenoptera); not printed in the passages read. source.authors: Seiya Tsujiuchi, Elena Sivan-Loukianova, Daniel F. Eberl, Yasuo Kitagawa, Tatsuhiko Kadowaki
source.title: Dynamic Range Compression in the Honey Bee Auditory System toward Waggle Dance Sounds

method: laser Doppler vibrometry: mechanical sensitivity of the antennal flagellum to pure tones of various frequencies and intensities, 4 live and 2 dead (ethanol-injected, measured immediately after the in vivo response) bees, one antenna per animal
conditions: Extracellular sound-evoked potentials (SEPs) recorded from the antennal nerve with the flagellar vibration velocity measured by laser Doppler vibrometer (CLV-700) and the air particle velocity by a near-field probe (Microflown); displacements calculated from the velocities (displacement = velocity/2πf). Bees: pollen foragers of unknown age unless otherwise noted (Methods default); colony, location and subspecies not stated (managed hive, accepted under audit 314). Vibrometry for this value: 4 live and 2 dead bees, one antenna each (the 'at least 5 animals' applies to the SEP recordings of line 3). Highest sensitivity at 350 Hz (suggested resonance); maximum mechanical sensitivity at low particle velocity, 0.3 to 4 mm/s; the post-mortem flagellum was comparable to in vivo in both magnitude and non-linearity, so the tuning and compression are passive mechanics. Control: SEPs were no longer detectable after pedicel lesion, so they are attributable to the Johnston's organ (JO). JO responses were lower in newly eclosed (0-day) bees than in 21-day-old foragers; which age group the 20 nm threshold in Fig. 6D comes from is not stated in the passages read. Responses saturate at flagellar tip displacement above 200 nm at 265 Hz (Fig. 6 legend). No temperature reported; no formal statistical test reported (page summary).
value: flagellar mechanical sensitivity specifically high for low-intensity stimuli of 265-350 Hz, not high-intensity stimuli
quote: The mechanical sensitivities of the antennal flagellum are specifically high in response to low but not high intensity stimuli of 265–350 Hz frequencies.
note: Abstract sentence; the Results (not read in full) give resonance near 350 Hz and saturation of the JO response above 200 nm tip displacement at 265 Hz. source.title: Hyperacute Directional Hearing and Phonotactic Steering in the Cricket (Gryllus bimaculatus deGeer)

method: behavioural: open-loop trackball steering of walking females to a computer-generated calling song played from frontal angles
conditions: Laboratory-reared females (reared individually from the last instar in the Cambridge colony); 15 phonotactically active females, each tested 3 times on consecutive days, at frontal angles up to 30 degrees either side with 0 degrees as each animal's reference; a second group of 15 animals had stimulation angles (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 20 degrees) randomly varied in order and direction to control for order effects; calling-song model with a 4.8 kHz carrier calibrated with a 1/4-inch free-field microphone at the cricket's position and adjusted to 75 dB SPL (measured stimulus); steering response to 1 degree differed from the response to 0 degrees (t-test, p = 0.01); the steering response of all tested animals was significantly directed to the side of stimulation (Results); at 30 degrees the relative steering response was 186% (25.3 cm/min). Already at 1 degree only 67% of the crickets consistently deviated towards the stimulated side; from 8 to 30 degrees (Results; the Discussion says from 6 degrees) the animals increasingly understeered, mean steering at 30 degrees only 11.3 +/- 5.6 degrees; total number of females tested before the 15 phonotactically active ones were selected not stated. Laboratory colony of the Cambridge Zoology Department, founding stock not stated (accepted at species rank, audit 332). Only the calling-song carrier tested; no sham or silent control beyond the 0 degree reference was described.
value: females walked towards the sound source at angles of sound incidence between 1 and 6 degrees
quote: Moreover, for angles of sound incidence between 1° and 6° the females precisely walked towards the sound source.
note: Directional hearing and steering rather than a detection threshold. Family and order from main (Gryllus bimaculatus rows: Gryllidae, Orthoptera). source.title: Hyperacute Directional Hearing and Phonotactic Steering in the Cricket (Gryllus bimaculatus deGeer)

method: laser vibrometry of tympanic membrane oscillations to sound from 30 degrees azimuth (binaural response difference)
conditions: Laboratory-reared Gryllus bimaculatus females (Cambridge colony); vibrometry stimulus 4.8 kHz carrier, 75 dB SPL reference level (page summary); only the left tympanic membrane was measured, in 10 experiments (4 also with summed afferent recordings), in tethered preparations with the thoracic ganglia removed and glass nanobeads on the posterior tympanum; the binaural difference was calculated 'Assuming a symmetric response function of both ears', not measured on both ears; 30 degrees is the largest angle tested; the same paper's behavioural experiment used 15 females tested on 3 consecutive days (see companion record).
quote: For tympanic membrane oscillations the binaural response difference was 12.9±2.7 dB at 30°.
note: Mean plus or minus value as printed (SD or SEM not stated in the passages read; n = 10 experiments).
